definition: The temporary assembly of high-pressure gate valves and spools installed on the wellhead for the duration of fracturing, wireline, and drillout work.
The multi-inlet flow head at the top of the frac tree where the high-pressure lines from the zipper manifold or missile combine into the well.
A valved manifold that lets one pump spread treat several wells on a pad in alternation without moving iron.
A tool stabbed through the wellhead or tree to carry abrasive treating fluid past the hanger seals and spool bores.
A two-position, through-conduit valve with a slab gate that slides across the bore between floating seats.
High-pressure temporary piping, swivels, and fittings with hammer unions used between the missile, zipper manifold, and tree.
The lowest valve on the tree, kept open and not cycled under pressure; the last barrier before the wellhead.
The top valve on the tree that gives vertical access for wireline and coiled tubing through a lubricator.
A horizontal valve on the tree cross that connects the well to the frac line or the flowback line.
The automatic pump shutdown that trips when treating pressure reaches the set maximum.
Proppant bridging in the perforations or near-wellbore fracture so that pressure rises rapidly at constant rate and proppant can no longer be placed.
The stage-by-stage completion method that sets a frac plug and perforates the next interval in one wireline run, then fractures through the new perforations.
The pressure-rated tube assembly above the tree that holds the tool string while the well is under pressure.
Hydraulic rams that close around the cable to seal the well with the tool string in the hole.
The head at the top of the lubricator where grease injected between the cable and close-fitting flow tubes holds back well pressure while the cable moves.
A hydraulic flapper below the lubricator that stops the tool string from falling back into the well if it parts from the cable.
Pumping fluid down the well to carry the plug-and-perf tool string along the horizontal lateral where gravity cannot.
The threaded collar joint between lubricator sections and stack components, sealed with an O-ring and made up by hand or hydraulically.
Two or more wells completed in alternation: one well is pumped while wireline sets the next plug and guns on its neighbor, so the spread never waits.
Two (simul), three (trimul), or four (quad) wells pumped at the same time from one spread through a split manifold, with wireline working ahead on the remaining wells.
The hydraulic valve above the cross and below the inlet block on the standard stack; isolates the well from the inlet block and the swab valve above it.
The flanged block above the crown valve where the spooled treating line from the zipper manifold enters the stack; replaces the goat head and its hammer-union iron.
The set-and-mill (or dissolve) isolation plug that seals the casing below a new stage so the fracture treatment goes only into the new perforations.
The wireline tool that converts a slow gas charge into the stroke that sets the frac plug, then shears free.

The manifold trailer in the middle of the pump rows: low-pressure suction headers on the outside edges feed the pumps; the high-pressure discharge header down the middle collects their output into one treating line.
The unit that mixes water, proppant, and chemicals into slurry at the rate the pumps take it, using a tub with augers and suction and discharge pumps.
The chain-driven gripper machine on top of the coiled tubing stack that pushes the coil into the well against pressure and pulls it out.
The hydraulic elastomer seal around the moving coiled tubing that keeps well pressure in while the coil runs.
The coiled tubing blowout preventer with blind, shear, slip, and pipe rams stacked in one body.
The skid of plug valves and chokes that takes the well from treating pressure down to separator pressure during flowback, with two runs so one choke can be changed while the other flows.
The pressure vessel that drops proppant and plug debris out of the flowback stream before the chokes and separator erode.
The permanent valve assembly set on the tubing head after the completion: masters, flow cross, wing valves, choke, and swab valve that control the producing well.
The check-valve fittings at the bottom of a casing string that guide it into the hole and keep cement from flowing back up the casing after the job.
The cement placed in the annulus between the casing and the hole (or the previous casing) that supports the string and isolates the formations behind it.
The fail-closed valve in the tubing below the wellhead that shuts the well in if surface control pressure is lost.
The per-well riser off the zipper header: a lower isolation valve and an upper working valve in series, then an elbow and outlet toward that well's tree.
The magazine on top of the frac tree that releases graduated frac balls into the flow one at a time for sliding sleeve completions.
A multistage completion where frac sleeves run in the casing are opened one at a time by dropping balls of increasing size, instead of setting plugs and perforating with wireline.
Pounds of proppant pumped per foot of lateral; with fluid intensity (bbl/ft) it sizes the sand and water logistics for the pad.
Lateral length divided by stage count; tighter spacing means more stages, more wireline runs or balls, and more time on the pad.
Any method that adds energy to lift fluid from a well that will not flow on its own: a beam unit stroking a rod pump, an electric submersible pump, injected gas, or a plunger.

The two check valves of a rod pump: the standing valve in the barrel opens on the upstroke to fill it, the traveling valve in the plunger opens on the downstroke so the plunger passes through the fluid it will lift on the next upstroke.
A sand control completion in which sized gravel is packed around a screen so the formation sand bridges on the gravel and the gravel is held by the screen.
A base pipe wrapped with keystone wire on ribs, leaving a slot narrower than the gravel or the formation sand it must hold.

The preventers bolted on the wellhead while a rig has pipe in the hole: an annular that closes on anything, pipe rams that close on the pipe, blind rams that close on an open hole, and a spool with kill and choke outlets.
Installing (nipple up) or removing (nipple down) the BOP stack or the tree on the wellhead, with the pressure test that follows.
The control room trailer where the treater runs the job from live pressure, rate, and density readings and the pump controls.
The sized sand or ceramic pumped into the fracture to hold it open after the pressure comes off; sized by mesh, chosen by closure stress.

A stop-work called when lightning is detected inside the pad's ten-mile ring: pumps down, rate to zero, crews off the pad to shelter, no work on iron. The all clear comes thirty minutes after the last strike inside the ring; the Simulator compresses the hold to sixty seconds.
